evidence.claim: Two bridges carry NC 24/27/73 across the Pee Dee River and Lake Tillery under the James B. Garrison name.
evidence.quote: The James B. Garrison Bridge are two automobile bridges spanning the Pee Dee River/Lake Tillery, between Stanly and Montgomery Counties.  The bridges carry NC 24/NC 27/NC 73.

evidence.claim: The older of these opened in 1927, replacing a 1922 bridge threatened by the new reservoir.
evidence.quote: The second and current westbound bridge opened in 1927, replacing the first Swift Island Ferry Bridge.

evidence.claim: Before the water rose, the Army tried to destroy the original with weight, aerial bombs and artillery.
evidence.quote: first by overloading with weight, second by aerial bombing and third by artillery.

evidence.claim: Explosives at its base finally brought it down.
evidence.quote: The fourth attempt was finally successful after placing 2,000 pounds (910 kg) of explosives, placed at the bases of the structure, detonating the bridge.

evidence.claim: The lake submerged its remains in 1928; the surviving 1927 bridge gained a parallel crossing in 1979.
evidence.quote: In 1928 the lake formed, submerging what little remained of the first bridge.

evidence.claim: the surviving 1927 bridge gained a parallel crossing in 1979.
evidence.quote: On July 13, 1979, the older 1927 bridge and new 1979 bridge were dedicated

evidence.claim: Longleaf pine forests supplied much of Troy’s early economy, with trees harvested for lumber and turpentine.
evidence.quote: Troy lies in an area once known for its vast longleaf pine forests; much of the town's early development came from the harvesting of those trees for lumber and turpentine.

evidence.claim: The Asheboro and Aberdeen Railroad and nearby gold mining accelerated growth in the late nineteenth century.
evidence.quote: The coming of the Asheboro and Aberdeen Railroad as well as the gold mining industry surrounding the town accelerated growth in the late 19th century.

evidence.claim: Textile mills and lumber mills contributed heavily to the economy in the twentieth century.
evidence.quote: By the 20th century textile mills and lumber mills were contributing heavily to Troy's economy.

evidence.claim: The county courthouse dates from 1921: a three-story tan-brick building with a columned portico and a clock in its triangular pediment.
evidence.quote: built in 1921.  It is a three-story, rectangular tan brick building in the Classical Revival style.  It features a pedimented tetrastyle Doric order pedimented portico  with a clock in the tympanum of the pediment.

evidence.claim: The Tyson & Jones Buggy Company manufactured carts and buggies here in the late nineteenth century.
evidence.quote: The town was the home of the Tyson & Jones Buggy Company, a predominant cart and buggy manufacturer in the late 1800s.

evidence.claim: The former plant burned a few years after it closed.
evidence.quote: A few years after being closed, the former Tyson Buggy plant burned down.

evidence.claim: The town’s spring Buggy Festival displays old Tyson buggies alongside tractors, hot rods and local pottery crafts.
evidence.quote: The town has an annual event in spring called the Buggy Festival. This event is used to showcase the history of the town and features music, hot rods, old tractors, old buggies made by the Tyson Buggy Company, and crafts from potteries in the surrounding areas.

evidence.claim: It takes place in the square by the Old Court House.
evidence.quote: The festival is held in the town square around the Old Court House

evidence.claim: The Moore County Courthouse was built in 1922–1923, with limestone facing and arched windows at its base.
evidence.quote: It was built in 1922–1923, and is a three-story, rectangular, limestone-faced building in the Renaissance Revival style.  It has a rusticated base pierced by arched paired windows

evidence.claim: The first bridge had three concrete arches; its replacement used four, each spanning 210 feet.
evidence.quote: The bridge consisted of three 146.2-foot (44.6 m) arches

evidence.claim: The town occupies a hilltop, with drainage running toward the Little River. NC 24/27 passes south of town, while its business routes enter the center.
evidence.quote: The town sits on a hilltop which drains southwest toward Warner Creek, a tributary of Rocky Creek, part of the Little River watershed leading to the Pee Dee River; north to Suck Branch, a tributary of Densons Creek, also leading to the Little River; and to the southeast by direct tributaries of the Little River.

flags: Partial overview: both NCDOT guidebook caches stop before the Sandhills chapter. The table of contents confirms inclusion but route-specific designation rationale, driving time, mileage and road character are unavailable. Intro kept shorter rather than padded.

Dropped unsupported current claims: Scots settlement from the Cape Fear, sandy-soil explanation, 46.2 miles, under-an-hour drive, logging nearly finishing longleaf pine in 1895, and views of Horse Trough and Shelter mountains.
Omitted the Henry Ford legend: the cache explicitly says it lacks evidence and contradicts Ford’s biography.
Lake Tillery page conflates bridge generations; used the dedicated bridge history to distinguish the demolished 1922 bridge from the 1927 replacement. Current lane configuration omitted.
Eastbound order follows increasing strip-map miles, reversing the current draft. Carthage lies beyond Biscoe in the cached road descriptions. No primary bridge-history source is cached.
